A rendering/layout engine turns HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into the visible page
Everyday features: tabs, bookmarks/favorites, history, autofill, downloads, back/forward navigation
Extensions/add-ons extend the browser and, because they can read and change page data, can pose security and privacy risks

claims.claim: A web browser is a program that retrieves and displays pages from the web and lets users follow hyperlinks to more pages; it is the most familiar kind of user agent.
A browser uses a rendering (layout) engine to turn the HTML, CSS, and JavaScript it receives into the page the user sees.

Browser extensions (WebExtensions) are add-ons built from HTML, CSS, and JavaScript that can modify page content and appearance and access browser features such as tabs, bookmarks, cookies, and history through a manifest permission system, giving them elevated privileges beyond an ordinary web page.
Because extensions can be granted permission to read and change data on the pages a user visits, a malicious or compromised extension is a real security and privacy risk.

HTTPS/TLS provides confidentiality, authenticity (server identity via a certificate), and integrity of data in transit, protecting against man-in-the-middle interception; the padlock indicates an encrypted, certificate-verified connection but does not guarantee the site itself is honest or safe.

Private/incognito browsing deletes local traces (history, cookies, and site data from the session) after the window closes, but it does not make the user anonymous, does not hide their IP address, and does not stop their ISP, employer, school, or the websites they visit from seeing their activity; nor does it protect against malware.
Keeping software up to date—especially web browsers—fixes security risks, and turning on automatic updates is a recommended way to stay patched.
As of July 2026 (worldwide, StatCounter), Chrome held roughly 68% of the browser market, Safari about 16%, Edge about 5%, and Firefox about 3%.

sourceRecords.title: Browser (MDN Web Docs Glossary)
sourceRecords.notes: Defines a browser as a program that retrieves and displays web pages and follows hyperlinks, the most familiar user agent, using a rendering engine. Lists Safari, Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Opera as common browsers. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording copied.

sourceRecords.title: What are extensions? (MDN Web Docs)
sourceRecords.notes: Describes extensions as add-ons built from HTML/CSS/JS that can modify page content and appearance, block ads, and access browser features (tabs, bookmarks, cookies, history) via a manifest permission system with elevated privileges beyond ordinary web pages. Supports both the capability and the risk framing.

sourceRecords.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) — Practical security implementation guides (MDN)
sourceRecords.notes: States TLS provides confidentiality, authenticity (server identity via certificate), and integrity, defeating man-in-the-middle interception. Supports the point that the padlock means an encrypted, certificate-verified connection, not that the site's content or intentions are trustworthy.

sourceRecords.title: Browser Market Share Worldwide (StatCounter GlobalStats)
sourceRecords.notes: Worldwide browser share, July 2026 snapshot: Chrome 68.22%, Safari 16.47%, Edge 5.37%, Firefox 3.34%, Samsung Internet 2.06%, Opera 1.88%. Used as a dated, attributed data point; figures rounded in the lesson and explicitly dated.

sourceRecords.title: Incognito browser: What it really means (Firefox)
sourceRecords.notes: Mozilla's own explanation of private/incognito browsing: it deletes local session data (history, cookies) but does not hide activity from the ISP, employer, school, or visited sites, does not hide the IP address or make the user anonymous, and does not protect against malware. Directly supports the incognito-limits framing.

sourceRecords.title: Update Software (CISA Secure Our World)
sourceRecords.notes: CISA guidance: many software updates exist to fix security risks; install all updates, especially for web browsers and antivirus software, as soon as possible, and turn on automatic updates. U.S. government work, public domain. Page is labeled 'Archived Content' but reflects current Secure Our World advice.
